q1: SELECT b.name AS bar, COUNT(DISTINCT f.drinker) AS num_drinker, AVG(s.price) AS avg_price, (SELECT f1.drinker FROM frequents AS f1 WHERE f1.bar = b.name ORDER BY f1.times_a_week DESC, f1.drinker ASC LIMIT 1) AS most_reg_drinker FROM bar AS b LEFT JOIN frequents AS f ON b.name = f.bar LEFT JOIN serves AS s ON b.name = s.bar GROUP BY b.name ORDER BY num_drinker DESC, b.name ASC
q2: SELECT maintable.bar, total_num_drinker, avg_price, most_reg_drinker FROM (SELECT total.bar, total_num_drinker, avg_price FROM (SELECT bar, COUNT(DISTINCT drinker) AS total_num_drinker FROM (SELECT DISTINCT bar, drinker FROM frequents) AS cnt RIGHT JOIN (SELECT bar.name AS bar FROM bar) AS bar USING (bar) GROUP BY bar) AS total INNER JOIN (SELECT bar, avg_price FROM (SELECT bar.name AS bar FROM bar) AS bar LEFT JOIN (SELECT bar, AVG(price) AS avg_price FROM serves GROUP BY bar) AS average USING (bar)) AS average ON total.bar = average.bar) AS maintable INNER JOIN (SELECT frequents.bar, drinker AS most_reg_drinker FROM frequents, (SELECT bar, MAX(times_a_week) AS Maxdrinker FROM frequents GROUP BY bar) AS Maxvalues WHERE (frequents.bar = Maxvalues.bar) AND (times_a_week = Maxdrinker)) AS Maxdrinkers ON maintable.bar = Maxdrinkers.bar ORDER BY most_reg_drinker ASC, total_num_drinker DESC

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent due to the different ways they handle the calculation of the most regular drinker. Q1 uses a subquery to find the most regular drinker for each bar, while Q2 uses a join with a subquery that finds the maximum times_a_week for each bar and then selects the corresponding drinker.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when there are multiple drinkers with the same maximum times_a_week for a bar. In this case, Q1 will return the drinker with the smallest name, while Q2 will return the drinker with the largest name.
